newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Tense post-election dispute diffused in Nicaragua.
newsitem.headline: Tense post-election dispute diffused in Nicaragua.

text.p: A potentially explosive confrontation was diffused on Saturday when about 50 leftist Sandinistas protesting alleged election fraud agreed, under threat, to end their hour-long protest at Managua's vote-counting centre.

The protesters, led by Rev. Miguel Angel Casco, campaign chief of Sandinista mayoral candidate Carlos Guadamuz, agreed to withdraw after dozens of anti-riot police gave them a 20-minute deadline to end the protest.

The Sandinista Front, which is trailing the right-wing Liberal Alliance in the presidential vote count, has claimed that Nicaragua's Oct. 20 elections were riddled with irregularities. It has called for the annulment of the vote in the populous department (province) of Managua.

"We want to say to Nicaragua and the world that the Sandinistas are not in agreement with these elections, that we have been robbed of these elections," said Casco, who is also a candidate for the National Assembly.
Nicaragua remained tense as delays in the announcing of the official vote winners and allegations of fraud have threatened to produce political instability.

President Violeta Chamorro and the Catholic Church have urged Nicaraguans to remain calm and called on election authorities to announce winners to avoid potential unrest. Police have banned public demonstrations.

Liberal candidate Arnoldo Aleman, who leads former Sandinista President Daniel Ortega 49 to 38 percent in the preliminary vote count, has already declared himself president-elect and has named his cabinet.
But Ortega has refused to concede defeat, hinting at Liberal electoral fraud, and saying he will wait until election officials have reviewed the vote count for irregularities.
"The Sandinistas want to say to the world that we will not let them rob us of these elections, and we are not going to let the 'somocistas' return to power," Casco said.
The Sandinistas, who governed Nicaragua from 1979 to 1990 with Cuban and Soviet backing, have equated Aleman to former dictator Anastasio Somoza, who was toppled by the 1979 Sandinista revolution.
International observers and the head of Nicaragua's Supreme Election Council, Rosa Marina Zelaya, have said there was no evidence of widespread fraud.
